transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-13 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Alice Romero (LuminaEd CTO), Devon Chen (LuminaEd SRE), Priya Patel (LuminaEd Product)

Summary:
Quick console-led walkthrough focusing on tracing, request logs, and error analysis workflows. Customer cares about surfacing root cause for intermittent 500s and high tail latency on their prompt-embedding pipeline. Demo shows how to correlate request logs with trace spans and use the Console's error analysis to drive triage. Agreed to run a focused staging test and share security docs.

Topics covered:
- Where request logs live and how to query them (filters, search)
- Tracing spans: model-level vs per-request, KV cache hits, batching visibility
- Error analysis: grouping, fingerprinting, automatic rollback triggers
- Debugging flow: reproduce -> trace -> rollback/fallback -> postmortem
- Integrations: sending custom spans to Datadog/Honeycomb & exporting logs

Action items (captured in metadata): see action_items field.

Transcript body (timestamps approximate, auto-generated transcriptions may have errors):
[00:00:05] Jordan: All right folks, thanks for joining. We're going to run through the Console tracing and request-log flows — show how you'd triage a 500 or a latency spike. Maya's going to drive most of the demo.
[00:00:20] Maya: Hi everyone, hi Alice, hi Devon, Priya — good to meet you. I'll start by pulling up the request logs for LuminaEd production, but we'll also show a couple of staging examples. Quick note: I might say KV cash instead of KV cache, transcriber sometimes does that, apologies.
[00:00:35] Alice: No worries. The big pain for us is that every few hours we'll see a burst of 500s for the embeder service, and it's hard to tell if it's model saturation, bad input, or our upstream batching.
[00:00:50] Devon: Right and the other symptom is P95 jumps from 130ms to like 1.2s, so we need to know if it's queuing or kernel-level slowdown.
[00:01:05] Maya: Exactly. So first I'm in the Console -> Requests tab. You can filter by model, route, region, status code, and a free-text search. I'm going to filter for status:500 and model:open-mpt-7b (note: example).
[00:01:30] Maya: Ok I see a cluster of five 500s between 14:03 and 14:07 UTC. If you click one, it brings up the request detail pane which has the raw request payload, tokens generated, timing breakdown, and a link to the trace.
[00:01:45] Maya: The important bit is the timing waterfall — you can see per-stage timings: queue time, model compute, KV lookup, serialization. That helps tell if it's queuing or compute.
[00:02:10] Priya: Does the waterfall show batching delays? Like how many requests were batched together?
[00:02:20] Maya: Yes — we surface the batch size per inference call. For continuous batching, you'll see a 'batcher wait' stage which shows how long this request waited to be coalesced.
[00:02:35] Jordan: And for your workload, where embeddings and prompts are mixed, that stage is often the root cause.
[00:02:50] Devon: I see. In our logs we use a custom correlation id — can we bring that into the Console so we can tie our traces to Redwood traces?
[00:03:05] Maya: Absolutely. You can pass the transaction_id as a request header and we will show it in the request metadata. We also allow you to map your internal ID to the trace span so when you open a trace it shows both IDs.
[00:03:20] Alice: Great, we've been dropping the X-Request-ID sometimes, maybe that's why a few events look orphaned.
[00:03:30] Maya: Now I'm going to open the trace view. This is a flame-style timeline of spans. Top-level spans are the request to Redwood; nested spans show scheduling, batch formation, token generation, and model kernel steps if we have that level of visibility.
[00:03:50] [00:03:50] Maya: you might notice some span names are auto-generated and some come from our instrumentation. We also ingest custom spans if you send them.
[00:04:05] Devon: Can we see KV cache hits? That's important — a missed KV entry could bump compute time massively.
[00:04:15] Maya: Yes. There's a 'KV cache' span that includes hit/miss metadata and latency. In this trace the KV cache shows a 95% hit rate but two misses that align with the long compute spans.
[00:04:35] Priya: That's useful. Is there an easy way to detect regressions in KV hit rates over time?
[00:04:45] Maya: In Optimize we have a KV hit metric and you can create alerts on drops. But even from the Console you can export time series for hit rate and overlay it with P95.
[00:05:05] Jordan: Also wanted to point out the error analysis tab — it groups errors by fingerprint, shows the top stack traces or model responses that lead to a 500, and suggests likely causes like malformed prompt, size limit exceeded, or model OOM.
[00:05:25] Maya: I'll open error analysis now. You can see a grouping titled 'model OOM' with 18 occurrences. Each group lists a representative request with the raw input and the failure payload.
[00:05:40] Maya: The grouping algorithm is fuzzy — it uses response pattern and status plus a few heuristics. It's not perfect but it catches 80-90% of related failures.
[00:05:55] Alice: Can it differentiate between our client sending bad JSON and an upstream model crash?
[00:06:05] Maya: It uses both server-side stack traces and the status code. If the model returns a 5xx but the payload is malformed, you'll usually see a parsing error early in the span. We also surface model stderr when available.
[00:06:20] Devon: How long are logs retained by default? We need 90 days for audits.
[00:06:30] Jordan: Hosted defaults vary; for enterprise customers we can set retention windows, and for Private deployments you control retention. We'll share the exact retention tiers in the security doc.
[00:06:45] Priya: Is there a way to do bulk export for a postmortem?
[00:06:55] Maya: Yes — you can export a set of request logs and traces as a tarball or push to your S3. There's also a link to stream to Datadog or Honeycomb for long-term storage.
[00:07:15] [00:07:15] Devon: About streaming — what's the overhead? We can't add 200ms to our request path.
[00:07:25] Maya: Streaming is async; logs are batched and shipped off the critical path. The SDK writes to a local buffer and flushes, typical added latency is sub-millisecond on the request path.
[00:07:40] Jordan: Quick demo of a reproduction flow: find a failing request, open the trace, jump to batcher wait and model compute spans, then click 'related requests' to see other requests in the same batch.
[00:07:55] Maya: Here I click 'related requests' — you can see five sibling requests, two of which had high queue wait. That signals the batcher created a large batch which increased per-request latency.
[00:08:15] Priya: That matches our incidents where spikes happen right after a spike in concurrent users.
[00:08:25] Maya: Right — you can set autoscale policies that cap batch sizes or route traffic to a cheaper lower-latency variant.
[00:08:40] Alice: We talked about fallbacks earlier — can Console trigger automatic fallback to a smaller model if P95 crosses threshold?
[00:08:50] Maya: Yes, in the Routing & Rollouts config you can set a latency SLO and fallback policy. If the observed P95 exceeds threshold for N minutes, traffic can be shifted to a fallback model or region. We show the events that caused the shift in the audit log.
[00:09:10] Devon: Is that irreversible? We need to be able to manually approve rollbacks.
[00:09:15] Maya: It's configurable: automatic, manual, or manual with suggested action. You can also have canary windows.
[00:09:30] Jordan: I'd like to call out the request metadata pane where you can add your own annotations during an incident — you can flag requests as 'root cause candidate' which helps the postmortem.
[00:09:45] Priya: Nice. For our SLOs we care about model-level and end-user latency; can we compute both?
[00:09:55] Maya: Yes, you can compute end-to-end by correlating your upstream instrumentation with Redwood traces, or use Redwood's ingestion to compute request to response timings.
[00:10:10] Alice: Let's go deeper — show us a concrete incident.
[00:10:15] Maya: OK, opening a representative 500. [00:10:20] Maya: In the trace I can see a 900ms model compute span with large memory allocations shown in the model debug blob — almost certainly an OOM that precipitated a server-side 500.
[00:10:40] Devon: Can we see GPU metrics inline? Like GPU utilization per request?
[00:10:50] Maya: For dedicated pools we surface GPU utilization aggregates and per-instance histograms. We don't show per-request GPU counter at kernel granularity in the hosted product for privacy/perf, but we do show sufficient indicators like compute ms, memory pressure, and model OOM traces.
[00:11:10] Jordan: If you need deeper kernel-level logs, in Dedicated we can enable an extended profiling mode that adds a small overhead.
[00:11:22] Priya: How would we triage malformed prompts that cause model crashes?
[00:11:28] Maya: Error analysis will show the representative prompt snippet. We have a 'sanitize' step we recommend — a validation pre-check to drop or rewrite bad payloads. Also suggestion: limit token length at client side and enforce JSON schema.
[00:11:45] Alice: Ok, suppose we identify a bad client version — can we retroactively map errors to a deploy id?
[00:11:55] Maya: Yes, if your deploy id is passed as metadata, the Console allows grouping by that field so you can see error rates per deploy.
[00:12:10] [00:12:10] Devon: We have a pattern where an upstream retry loop double-submits requests — does Console detect duplicate requests?
[00:12:20] Maya: We have dedupe heuristics if the same payload and ID come within a short window; we surface that as 'duplicate submission' in the request detail. You can also create alerts when duplicate rate increases.
[00:12:40] Jordan: Quick sidebar: important to instrument and pass your correlation ids so nothing looks orphaned.
[00:12:50] Alice: Understood.
[00:13:05] Maya: Now I'm switching to the Alerts tab to show an example alert on P95. You can configure the threshold, evaluation window, and the action: Slack, webhook, or routing change.
[00:13:25] Priya: We'd prefer a webhook to our incident system and a slack notif to #platform-incidents — can do that?
[00:13:33] Maya: Yep. We support multiple hooks and per-alert silencing windows.
[00:13:45] Devon: A performance question — if we enable detailed tracing for a single customer, does that impact other tenants?
[00:13:55] Maya: No — tracing level is per-customer and isolated. Detailed profiling is limited to Dedicated customers if you need kernel traces.
[00:14:10] Alice: Can we restrict who at our org can see certain fields, e.g., model stderr containing sensitive tokens?
[00:14:20] Jordan: Console respects RBAC. For hosted, some sensitive fields are redacted by default; with Private you can decide retention and redaction. We can walk through the RBAC roles in the security doc.
[00:14:35] Maya: I'm going to simulate a tail latency spike in staging. (simulation) Now we see a window where P95 jumps; Console links that to a particular model version and region.
[00:14:55] [00:14:55] Maya: I trigger a synthetic request set and you can see the spans populate in near real-time in the trace viewer.
[00:15:10] Devon: Nice, the live tail view is helpful.
[00:15:20] Priya: Are there notebook exports so product can play with the data?
[00:15:25] Maya: Yes — you can export a CSV or use our API to pull data into a Jupyter notebook. We also have a sample notebook for root-cause analysis. Jordan: We'll send that link.
[00:15:35] Alice: About cost — if we enable per-request debugging and verbose logs, how does that affect billing?
[00:15:45] Jordan: Logs and extended traces are billable additional storage and ingestion; we'll include a cost estimate in the Dedicated pricing doc. There's also sampling so you can keep verbose logs for 1% of traffic.
[00:15:58] Devon: Sampling is good. For incidents we want to ramp sampling to 100% for 10 minutes; can that be done?
[00:16:05] Maya: Yes, you can set ephemeral sampling overrides during an incident window.
[00:16:18] Priya: One more thing — can Console surface data residency for logs? We need European logs stored in EU.
[00:16:25] Jordan: We support region-based retention and storage for Enterprise/Private. We'll include the data residency options in the follow-up package.
[00:16:40] Maya: Ok, wrapping up with runbook example: We have a templated incident response playbook that ties Console artifacts into steps — detection, triage, mitigation (roll back/fallback), postmortem. You can clone and customize it for your org.
[00:16:58] Alice: That would be very helpful.
[00:17:05] Maya: Final bit — exporting a postmortem: click 'Export incident' and it packages request logs, traces, alerts, and config snapshots. Works well for audits.
[00:17:18] Jordan: To recap real quick: next steps are Maya will run a tracing scenario against your staging (Devon/Maya), Jordan will send security and retention docs, and we'll follow up with Dedicated pricing options.
[00:17:35] Alice: Sounds good.
[00:17:40] Devon: One quick Q — if we find model OOMs are frequent, is the recommendation to quantize or shard the model?
[00:17:50] Maya: It depends — Optimize will suggest quantization profiles or a variant with smaller memory footprint; in some cases sharding or model partitioning helps. We'll review recommendations after the staging run.
[00:18:05] Priya: Thanks everyone.
[00:18:12] Jordan: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the links and the runbook.

(Transcript continues with a brief Q&A and wrap; auto-transcription shows occasional word swaps like 'K-B cache' for 'KV cache' and 'embeder' for 'embedder', minor punctuation inconsistencies.)

End of meeting.
